newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma rebels fear pressure from new Thai government.
newsitem.headline: Burma rebels fear pressure from new Thai government.

text.p: Ethnic minority Burmese rebels based on the border with Thailand said on Thursday they were afraid the new Thai government would pressure them to end their decades-old struggle with military rulers in Rangoon.

Members of different rebel organisations told Reuters they were worried because Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, set to become Thailand's next prime minister, was a former army chief with close ties to Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC).

Representatives of the Karen National Union (KNU) guerrilla group said they were trying to speed up peace talks with SLORC representatives on the suggestion of a Thai general. They did not name the general.

The predominantly Christian KNU was formed in 1948 after Burma gained independence from Britain. It is the last major rebel group still fighting for autonomy despite several rounds of peace talks with the SLORC.
"A Thai general told us that we should speed up the negotiation with the SLORC since General Chavalit is about to be the new leader, " a senior KNU member told Reuters.

The KNU member said the group feared a repetition of what happened in 1989, when Chavalit spearheaded the repatriation of hundreds of Burmese dissidents who were living with the KNU in jungles near the border after fleeing a bloody coup in Rangoon.

The SLORC took power in 1988 after brutally suppressing pro-democracy demonstrations that swept the country. Thousands were killed or imprisoned during the uprising and thousands of others fled to border areas of neighbouring countries.
Returning refugees faced persecution, rebels said. Some had reportedly been killed and others arrested.
Members of the rebel Karenni National People Party (KNPP) and an executive member of the Shan State Organisation (SSO) said they also lived in fear.

"General Chavalit is very close to the SLORC and we anticipate that he will put the pressure on us in order to please the SLORC and to secure his personal interest," said Aung Mya, commander of the small KNPP guerrilla group.
He said he was afraid the new Thai administration would order officials to push back refugees who fled to Thailand.
The bases of the KNU and KNPP guerrillas are in the jungles of eastern Burma, but about 100,000 refugees have crossed the border and live in sprawling camps inside Thailand.
The SLORC has accused the guerrillas of hiding in refugee camps and of sometimes operating from them. The refugees have been the target of several attacks by troops from Burma.
An official responsible for assisting Shan refugees who now lives in the jungle on the Thai border also anticipates his job will be more difficult with the new Thai administration.
"For the time being they are still allowing us to pass the checkpoints to help the refugees, but I am not so optimistic after Chavalit becomes prime minister," a member of the SSO told Reuters.
